reviews.text: FIX YOUR CLERIC. A setting similar to Dungeon Keeper, text quests just like in Space Rangers, a faction system for your minions. A unique indie game that clearly needs more publicity.

Good simple game for $5, but game design leaves a lot to be desired. - Individual battles, especially in the beginning, are extremely skewed. 90% of the time, you won't do any meaningful damage to the heroes, and the other 10% of the time, when you've weakened them outside of battle, they won't be able to do anything meaningful to your units. - Unit AI is extremely stupid, even for an auto-battler. - Like the other English review mentions, the hero Cleric is broken strong, easily able to heal the hero party to 100% each battle, while your units die for nothing because they can't directly target the Cleric. - Sadist with Seed of Darkness is similarly broken, perhaps even more so (every rest spot, the hero party is healed to 100% health and sanity) - Despite these flaws, it's extremely easy to break this game once you figure out the ropes. Just pick Politician as your lord, keep making positive choices to increase all factions' friendliness, use Mutilation Magic on heroes every rest spot. This will result in the Ratfolk gradually gnawing away at the heroes' provisions, making them Desperate, which makes them easy pickings for the Ratfolk instakill ability. That said, I had to stop playing because of a game breaking bug. I had only a Hunter with 2 Brink of Deaths make it to the final round (he'd have been extremely easy to kill), but the game just crashes loading the last round. I'm hardstuck (other than wiping meta-progress entirely) because I'm on True Death mode, which disables New Game for some dumb reason (just treat starting a New Game as a Defeat, duh)

It's a nice narrative game, with a lot of (possibly AI) art, and well written choice-based text events. Gets some time and effort to get into, and the replayability isn't really there (it doesn't really work as a roguelike, and the events are pretty deterministic, so they get familiar). But it was a nice experience for the first 5 hours.
Decent game, like a more hands on version of Sort the Court. But the only game mode at the moment are quick matches, when really I would've liked something that went on for longer.

Great concept deeply hampered by obnoxious rules (the heroes have a "Nuh uh, I don't die, in fact I get all my health back *and* I have a huge buff that insures you're likely to lose" mechanic), and most events being designed to punish you for not winning RNG. There's even an event that gives you absolutely nothing -- unless you pick the wrong option, then you get a lowered opinion of one of your factions.

Delightful and cheap game about being an evil overlord. While not that deep this game offers enjoyable time trying to overcome bands of heroes invading your peaceful tyranny. This game offers some strategic depth and choices as you have to choose how you plan on defeating each hero and how to use resources to do that - having to have some stores of gold and mana to deal with political considerations, fighting heroes and other potential uses. Honestly this feels like a proper computer game with interesting gameplay - it has refreshingly unique feeling to it that I deeply appreciate as too many games feel like copies of each other as games attempt to perfect some particular formula, and that is sufficient to make this game worth buying in my opinion. It is short and it has some interesting story elements creating an unique experience that accomplishes telling short stories about particular lich trying to fend off bands of heroes. After a while you learn what each option for each event does, but at that point I feel this game has entertained me enough for its price.

Really cool concept. I had fun playing this one for a bit. I got through one play through, I may go through some more. Some of the decisions I had to make weren't clear on what the outcome would actually impact. It could be I just wasn't paying enough attention, and if they went negatively I just shrugged and trekked on. I am not a big fan of the RNG-based outcomes, but it wasn't enough for me to turn this review to a negative.
Fun game. More complex than I thought it would be, in a good way. Lots of learning to be done and new things pop up even after 7 hours in. Well worth the money.
interesting game, definitely not for everyone, but still fun. art is amazing

A nice little game with D&D/fantasy elements. The different heroes and starting options offer some variety, even if some events are repetitive. The main story reveals itself after winning a few games.

Excellent beginnings of a game, the story selections are interesting, but limited as it is still only 0.1 EA. The auto battler system is functional and not terrible to watch, AI seems to B line for the front line regardless of placement, which is unfortunate and removes any strategic depth. Overall, I played through a bit of the game and will be happy to return in a year when the game has been fleshed out (if I am still here, darn ALS might get me first) I recommend this game for a few reasons, the developer is consistent and cares, the price is ridiculously low a friggen mcdonalds hamburger is the same price now, and to keep this gentleman that made this game going financially. Good luck to you all and God Bless
It's a short and sweet 12-ish hour rogue-lite with a few interesting mechanics. I picked up for $4 and it was worth it.

Simple: This game is fun and if you like D&D or anything similar, I recommend it. I watched a YouTuber play and thought it looked fun. I had the idea to play it with two friends as if I was the "dungeon master" and they were the players. They were the bad guy, of course. So reverse D&D, if you will. I loaded up the game and streamed it to them while they made decisions. This was an awesome way to play! Great cheap way to have at least a few hours of good times with friends. For the price of entry, can't go wrong. Try it out. Since that first session I have played through myself a few times and I'm really enjoying it. Sure, there are a few typos, balance could use some work, and this affordable game is not perfect. What game is? So far I've seen a ton of unique events in each play through, there are multiple ways to win, there are lots of unexpected twists, and I'm really enjoying it. If you aren't scared of reading a little text, there are several hours of fun ahead. Overall, I hope the developer will keep updating the game, but I recommend it as is! Edit: Oh and I forgot to mention there is even an evolving sub plot as you complete play throughs! It's really intriguing and creepy. I definitely want to figure out what is going on.

An interesting game that seems simple at first but has quite a bit more going on under the hood the more you play. You are an evil overlord who has a number of days to defeat a party of heroes that are coming to defeat you. You have a number of options on each day on what to do, you can fight the heroes, gather resources/artifacts to increase your power, improve your standing with the various factions in your kingdom (each of which contribute units and bonuses to your kingdom depending on how much in favor you are with them) and also take part in events in which you pick various options. There interesting thing is that beating the heroes is not just about defeating them in battle (although that is an option). You can weaken them over time by stealing their supplies and denying them more so they slowly starve, you can lower their morale so they just abandon the quest or possibly even turn them against each other. But on the flip side, the factions in your kingdom can also turn against you, refusing to help you or even helping the heroes. So there is a lot of gears and levels you can move to affect things. Furthermore, as you get in game achievements you open up new starting options, such as starting a game with different levels of support from various factions, or starting with different levels of resources. You can also pick different hero party compositions to fight against as well as their personalities (different personalities will affect the outcome of events and the likelyhood of you being able to manipulate individual heroes). All in all the game has a lot more than I first thought when I jumped in just expecting a auto battler defense type game. I've completed 2 full runs so far along with a couple failed ones that I restarted after making some major mistakes as I was still learning how things worked. I enjoyed it.

Man now I feel bad about all the bosses I've killed in other games. Pretty good. It mixes text-based decision making with some basic strategy mechanics making it more engaging than pure text-based decision games like For The Queen or Yes Your Grace. However, there's no random element to the events so the game will get a bit repetetive as you encounter the same event again and again and learn the best choice. This is both good and bad as the results make sense but it also makes playthroughs more samey. It's not a revolutionary title but it's mostly charming and the events and political choices are decently thought out. Except for the r**e events, not a fan of those. I'm an evil lich, not a monster. The price is pretty fair. If you like the premise you should get it.

Great game if you enjoy playing from the perspective of an evil protagonist, you essentially lay out troops from four separate factions (Goblins, Rat-kin, Lizard-folk, and Cultists + your own skeletons as a lich). Each faction has their own interests and "morals" that you have to either balance to maintain favor, or completely ignore and punish to command fear. There are multiple ways to combat the heroes outside of pure combat, and the story strikes a good balance between fun and grim. My only real complaint is that there isnt any way to direct troops during combat, meaning you have to leave all movement up to the ai which can be mildly frustrating.

The game has a good grasp on what makes choices enjoyable, the results are predictable, they can chain and they can be taken back with another choice. The game gives your choices consequences, with your minions sabotaging you when oppressed. Overall the story choices part of the game is well done. The combat can be janky at times, with your units focusing on the wrong enemy, I'd be nice to see different priorities between units. But you're not supposed to win every fight, just damage the enemy. It's a simple system that only supports another part of the game instead of having its own depth. The last part of the game is the sabotage you get to do when the enemy rests. This system works well, you need to plan ahead and mechanically all the choices are there, but there's a lot of story opportunity that wasn't captured here. You either torment the heroes or end up bribing them, there's little nuance to it other than the random hero traits that make one of the options more likely. Overall the game is good fun, a little easy to figure out, but the different titles and hero parties change it up a fair bit. It could use some more complexity when it comes to the tactics and the sabotage, but the lack of it doesn't make the game any less enjoyable.

To me it feels like a visual novel with "choice matters" moments. The story and the events are fun if static; each event is the same each time, influenced by your choices, faction relationship, hero type/traits; so while the same, there is variability in the outcomes. The autobattle component is the weakest aspect of the game, with little varity in battle maps and very simple unit pathing/attack simply selecting the closest target, lead to a degree of annoyance. But is one of the main limitation of autobattle engagements. Being able to set your Overlord preset provides a different story arc, weighting events differently increasing/decreasing occurrence; altering Hero party composition influences event outcomes and susceptibility to certain "rest time" activity. The pixel art is nothing special, though the rest of the pieces within the game are wonderful. For the price of ~$10AUD I have found it worth my time and attention.

This is mostly a text based game with some minor stratagy battle sequences. I have never been so compelled to read text in a game as I have with this one. Its a fun relaxing game and reverses roles for your classic D&D set up. For what it is, 10/10 for me

Slay or Fall is a thoughtfully constructed indie strategy game that places narrative choice and long-term consequence at the center of its design. Developed by ostsergey and published by Ostsergey Games, the game flips a familiar fantasy trope by casting the player not as a wandering hero, but as the Dark Lord presiding over a vast dungeon under constant threat. Rather than relying on visuals or action-heavy mechanics, Slay or Fall builds tension through text, systems, and decisions that steadily accumulate weight as each run progresses. The core structure is roguelike in spirit but narrative in execution. Each playthrough unfolds as a sequence of events, crises, and opportunities that must be navigated before the inevitable final confrontation with invading heroes. Progress is not measured in experience points or loot, but in survival, stability, and influence. Every decision you make—whether diplomatic, cruel, pragmatic, or manipulative—pushes the world in subtle but meaningful directions. Failure often comes not from a single bad choice, but from compounding consequences that reveal themselves only after several turns, reinforcing the game’s emphasis on foresight and restraint. A defining feature of Slay or Fall is its faction system, which adds a layer of political management to the narrative flow. Your dungeon is inhabited by several distinct groups, each with their own priorities and attitudes toward your rule. Goblins may boost wealth but strain order, Cultists offer loyalty and magical power at moral cost, Lizards provide military strength and discipline, and Ratfolk thrive on subterfuge and instability. Balancing these factions is rarely straightforward, as empowering one often alienates another. The tension between maintaining internal cohesion and preparing for external threats creates a constant push-and-pull that drives the game forward. Events are the heart of the experience, and they are impressively varied and reactive. Moral dilemmas, strategic opportunities, betrayals, and unexpected twists emerge regularly, often influenced by earlier choices or the current state of your factions. These events rarely present obvious “correct” answers, instead asking players to commit to a philosophy of rule and accept the risks that come with it. Over time, the game begins to feel less like a puzzle to be solved and more like a story shaped by your leadership style, whether that style leans toward tyranny, cunning diplomacy, or calculated cruelty. Although combat exists within Slay or Fall, it is abstracted and contextual rather than tactical in a traditional sense. Outcomes are determined largely by preparation, faction strength, and prior decisions, reinforcing the idea that battles are won long before swords are drawn. This approach keeps the focus on strategy and narrative cohesion, ensuring that combat feels like a consequence of your rule rather than a separate mechanical challenge. When things go wrong, it is usually clear why, even if the realization comes too late to undo the damage. Presentation is intentionally minimal, with a clean interface designed to keep the player’s attention on text and choice rather than spectacle. This restraint works in the game’s favor, as it allows the writing and systems to carry the experience without distraction. Accessibility options and clear UI elements make long sessions comfortable, and the absence of visual clutter helps reinforce the sense that you are overseeing events from a distant, commanding perspective rather than acting directly within them. Replayability is one of Slay or Fall’s greatest strengths. Because so many events branch based on prior decisions, faction balance, and randomization, no two runs play out the same way. Early failures often feel instructive rather than punishing, encouraging experimentation and different leadership approaches in subsequent attempts. Over time, players begin to recognize patterns, anticipate consequences, and refine strategies, giving the game a satisfying learning curve despite its text-heavy nature. Ultimately, Slay or Fall succeeds by trusting its audience to engage deeply with its systems and narrative. It does not rush, overexplain, or simplify its ideas, instead offering a dense web of choices that reward careful thought and reflection. For players who enjoy text-driven strategy, moral decision-making, and emergent storytelling, it delivers a rich and replayable experience that proves tension and drama can thrive without action-heavy mechanics. Slay or Fall is less about conquering the world outright and more about surviving it on your own terms—and that focus gives it a distinct and memorable identity within the indie strategy space. Rating: 8/10
A fun text roguelike designed for many runs. Many presets, various heroes, text events with different outcomes and consequences - all this makes you come back to the game again and again!
(Early access) A dungeon-keeper type game, where the tower defense action sequences are alterned with quests and decision-making problems in a rather good narrative setting
A really captivating roguelike game with a huge potential, which has a lot to offer even at the early access stage! There are some technical flaws, but It won't spoil the overall impression.
Slay or Fall is very atmospheric in its design and excels greatly in its mix of gameplay and story telling through the multiple dialogue choices. This is a great game to play at your own speed.

Play as a dark lord defending his dungeon from venturing heroes. A text-based management game where you must summon and command your minions to fight humans. Has ratfolk units you can control.
